factors.definition: Return on small-cap portfolio minus return on big-cap portfolio. Stocks sorted by market equity (ME = price * shares outstanding) at June end; small = below NYSE median, big = above. SMB = (1/3)(S/H + S/M + S/L) - (1/3)(B/H + B/M + B/L)

factors.definition: Return on high B/M portfolio minus return on low B/M portfolio. Stocks sorted by book-to-market equity (BE/ME); high = top 30%, low = bottom 30%. HML = (1/2)(S/H + B/H) - (1/2)(S/L + B/L)
factors.source_paper: Quantitative Issue - 3 팩터 모델의 한국시장 분석 (전편) - Fama-French 92년 논문의 한국시장 적용 결과.pdf

factors.definition: Excess return of the market portfolio over the risk-free rate. Rm - Rf where Rm = value-weighted return of all stocks, Rf = risk-free rate (e.g., T-bill rate or CD rate for Korea)

factors.definition: BE/ME = Book equity / Market equity. Book equity = total shareholders equity + deferred taxes - preferred stock. Market equity = stock price * shares outstanding

factors.definition: Natural log of market equity. ME = Price * Shares Outstanding. Negative relation with average returns: smaller firms earn higher returns
factors.source_paper: Quant Issue - 3 팩터 모델의 한국시장 분석 (후편) - Fama-French 93년 논문의 한국시장 적용 결과.pdf

factors.definition: EP = Earnings per share / Stock price. Positive E/P stocks earn higher returns. Related to value factor

FF5 profitability factor. RMW = return of stocks with robust (high) operating profitability minus return of stocks with weak (low) profitability. Operating profitability = (Revenue - COGS - SGA - Interest Expense) / Book Equity
factors.data_needed: revenue, cogs, sga, interest_expense, book_equity, monthly_returns

factors.definition: FF5 investment factor. CMA = return of stocks with conservative (low) asset growth minus return of stocks with aggressive (high) asset growth. Asset growth = (Total Assets_t - Total Assets_{t-1}) / Total Assets_{t-1}

Carhart 4-factor momentum. UMD = return on past winners minus return on past losers. Winners/losers defined by cumulative return from t-12 to t-2 (skip most recent month). Long top 30%, short bottom 30%
Beta from CAPM regression: R_i = alpha + beta * R_m + epsilon. Estimated using 60 months of trailing returns. Measures systematic market risk exposure

TV_GG = FCFF_{t+1} / (WACC - g), where g = retention_rate * ROIC. Investment strategy: buy stocks trading below terminal value estimate. Uses historical financials (5yr avg margins, ROIC) to eliminate analyst optimism bias
factors.data_needed: fcff, wacc, roic, retention_rate, revenue, operating_margin

factors.definition: TV_VD = NOPAT_{t+1} * (1 - g/ROIC) / (WACC - g). Alternative DCF terminal value using value driver formula. Tends to select higher-quality value stocks (higher margins, higher ROIC) compared to Gordon Growth

Expected excess return on equity over bonds. Estimated via: (1) historical approach using long-run stock-bond return differential, (2) survey approach asking investors/managers, (3) implied approach using current equity prices and risk premiums in bond/real estate markets. Key determinants: investor risk aversion, information uncertainty, macro risk perceptions
factors.data_needed: stock_returns, bond_returns, risk_free_rate, equity_prices, default_spreads, cap_rates

factors.definition: Composite quality factor: QMJ = z(Profitability) + z(Growth) + z(Safety) + z(Payout). Long high-quality (safe, profitable, growing, well-managed) stocks, short low-quality junk stocks. Quality = z-score average of four components

z-score average of: GPOA (gross profit/assets), ROE (net income/equity), ROA (net income/assets), CFOA (cash flow from operations/assets), GMAR (gross margin = revenue-COGS/revenue), ACC (low accruals = earnings quality)
factors.data_needed: gross_profit, total_assets, net_income, equity, cfo, revenue, cogs, accruals

factors.definition: z-score average of 5-year growth rates in: GPOA growth, ROE growth, ROA growth, CFOA growth, GMAR growth. Growth rates computed as 5-year change in each profitability measure
factors.data_needed: gross_profit, total_assets, net_income, equity, cfo (5 years of history)

factors.definition: z-score average of: low market beta, low idiosyncratic volatility (residual vol from FF3), low leverage (debt/assets), low bankruptcy risk (Ohlson O-score or Altman Z-score), low earnings volatility (ROE std dev)
factors.data_needed: beta, idio_vol, total_debt, total_assets, roe_history, stock_returns

factors.definition: z-score average of: equity net issuance (negative = net buyback is good), debt net issuance (low is good), total net payout (dividends + buybacks - issuance). Measures shareholder-friendly capital allocation
GPOA = Gross Profit / Total Assets. Novy-Marx (2013) showed gross profitability is the cleanest accounting measure of true economic profitability and predicts cross-section of returns
ROE = Net Income / Shareholders Equity. DuPont decomposition: ROE = Net Profit Margin * Asset Turnover * Financial Leverage = (NI/Sales) * (Sales/Assets) * (Assets/Equity)
Net Profit Margin = Net Income / Revenue. One of the three DuPont components of ROE. Measures how efficiently a company converts revenue into profit
Asset Turnover = Revenue / Total Assets. DuPont component measuring efficiency of asset utilization
Financial Leverage = Total Assets / Shareholders Equity. DuPont component. High leverage boosts ROE but increases risk. Quality stocks should have stable/manageable leverage
Pillar 1 of multidimensional quality. Composite of: ROE, ROA, ROIC, Gross Margin, Net Margin, EBITDA Margin. Cross-sectional z-score average. Captures ability to generate returns from operations
factors.data_needed: roe, roa, roic, gross_margin, net_margin, ebitda, revenue, total_assets, equity, invested_capital

factors.definition: Pillar 2 of multidimensional quality. Measures earnings sustainability via accrual ratios. Low accruals = high earnings quality. Accruals = (Net Income - CFO) / Total Assets. Cash-based earnings are more persistent than accrual-based

Pillar 3 of multidimensional quality. Composite of: low leverage (Debt/Equity, Debt/Assets), low earnings volatility (std of ROE), low beta, low idiosyncratic volatility. Important during market turmoil (GFC, Covid-19)
factors.data_needed: total_debt, equity, total_assets, roe_history, beta, idio_vol

factors.definition: Pillar 4 of multidimensional quality. Measures capital discipline via asset growth, capex/assets, R&D intensity. Conservative investment = higher future returns (negative relation). Asset Growth = (TA_t - TA_{t-1}) / TA_{t-1}
Cash-based operating profitability = (Revenue - COGS - SGA + R&D - Accruals) / Total Assets. Ball et al. (2016) showed cash-based profitability subsumes accrual-based measures in predicting returns
factors.data_needed: revenue, cogs, sga, rnd_expense, accruals, total_assets

factors.definition: Enhanced momentum signal that conditions on trend clarity. Trend clarity = R-squared of a linear trend regression on past returns (e.g., 12-month window). Stocks with high trend clarity (clear upward trend) have stronger momentum returns (12.68% annualized in top quintile vs 6.90% traditional). Trend Clarity = R^2 from regression of cumulative returns on time index
Mom12m = cumulative return from month t-12 to t-2 (skipping most recent month). Standard Jegadeesh-Titman momentum. Past winners continue to outperform past losers

Momentum signal based on financial analyst coverage network. Build a graph where edge weights = number of analysts jointly covering both firms. Use graph attention network to aggregate information from neighboring firms for spillover momentum prediction. Portfolio based on GNN predictions yields annualized 29.44% return, Sharpe 4.06

Narrative extracted from earnings calls that predicts realized earnings and analyst expectations. Uses LLM text-morphing methodology to generate counterfactual presentations that vary topical emphasis while holding quantitative content fixed. Captures prevailing narrative component of earnings calls beyond hard numbers

SUE = (Actual EPS - Forecast EPS) / std(Actual - Forecast). Measures earnings surprise standardized by historical forecast error volatility. Positive SUE predicts positive PEAD (Post-Earnings Announcement Drift). Used as key predictor alongside ML models

Abnormal returns in the 60-90 days following earnings announcement. Stocks with positive earnings surprises continue to drift upward, negative surprises drift downward. Related to slow information diffusion. Long-horizon retail investor composition amplifies PEAD

Ratio of long-horizon to short-horizon retail investors around earnings announcements. Measured from StockTwits self-reported holding periods. High long-horizon composition -> underreaction + larger PEAD. High short-horizon composition -> overreaction + reversal. Zero-cost strategy exploiting this heterogeneity earns significant alpha

Latent consensus features learned by deep learning bottleneck architecture from 114 firm characteristics + 123 macro indicators. Model learns to approximate analyst consensus (EPS forecasts, recommendations) as intermediate representation, then uses these to predict returns. Key consensus dimensions: Analyst Value, Analyst Optimism, Analyst EPS, EPS Forecast Revision, Change in Forecast and Accrual

Residual from modified Jones model regression of total accruals on change in revenue and PPE. High abnormal accruals predict negative future returns (Xie 2001). Accruals = (Change in CA - Change in Cash - Change in CL + Change in STD - Depreciation) / Lagged TA
factors.data_needed: current_assets, cash, current_liabilities, short_term_debt, depreciation, total_assets, revenue

factors.definition: Total Accruals = (Net Income - Cash Flow from Operations) / Total Assets. Sloan (1996) accrual anomaly: firms with high accruals earn lower future returns because accrual component of earnings is less persistent than cash component

EntMult = Enterprise Value / EBITDA. Enterprise Value = Market Cap + Total Debt - Cash. Loughran and Wellman (2011): low enterprise multiple stocks earn higher returns. More comprehensive value measure than P/E or B/M

AssetGrowth = (Total Assets_t - Total Assets_{t-1}) / Total Assets_{t-1}. Cooper, Gulen, Schill (2008): firms with high asset growth earn lower subsequent returns. Negative cross-sectional relation between asset growth and stock returns

IdioVol3F = standard deviation of residuals from FF3 model regression using daily returns over trailing month. Ang et al. (2006): high idiosyncratic volatility stocks earn lower subsequent returns (idiosyncratic volatility puzzle)

ILLIQ = (1/D) * Sum(|R_d| / Volume_d). Average ratio of absolute daily return to daily dollar volume. Higher values = more illiquid. Amihud (2002): illiquidity premium - illiquid stocks earn higher expected returns

IndMom = value-weighted return of stocks in the same industry over past 6-12 months. Grinblatt and Moskowitz (1999): industry momentum is distinct from individual stock momentum and adds incremental predictive power

IntMom = cumulative return from month t-12 to t-7. Novy-Marx (2012): intermediate-horizon past returns (months 7-12) are a better predictor than recent past returns. Distinct from and complementary to standard momentum
NOA = (Operating Assets - Operating Liabilities) / Total Assets. Hirshleifer et al. (2004): high NOA predicts lower future returns. Broad measure of balance sheet bloat capturing cumulative accruals

OPLeverage = (COGS + SGA) / Total Assets. Novy-Marx (2011): higher operating leverage amplifies exposure to systematic risk, earning a risk premium. Firms with high fixed costs have more volatile earnings
Leverage = Total Debt / Market Equity. Bhandari (1988): firms with higher leverage earn higher returns, consistent with financial risk compensation. Related to default risk premium

ResidualMomentum = cumulative residual return from FF3 model over months t-12 to t-2. Blitz, Huij, Martens (2011): momentum based on FF3 model residuals is more persistent and less crash-prone than raw price momentum

EarningsSurprise = (Actual EPS - Forecast EPS) / |Forecast EPS|. Foster, Olsen, Shevlin (1984): positive earnings surprises predict positive abnormal returns in subsequent quarter. Foundation of PEAD literature

EarningsConsistency = count of consecutive quarters with positive earnings growth / total quarters. Alwathainani (2009): firms with consistent earnings growth patterns earn higher returns. Measures earnings predictability

EarningsStreak = number of consecutive quarters of beating analyst consensus. Loh and Warachka (2012): longer streaks of positive surprises predict higher future returns due to anchoring bias in analyst expectations

RevenueSurprise = (Actual Revenue - Forecast Revenue) / |Forecast Revenue|. Jegadeesh and Livnat (2006): revenue surprises provide incremental predictive power beyond earnings surprises for future returns

TrendFactor = moving average signal aggregating multiple trend signals across different horizons (3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 days). Han, Zhou, Zhu (2016): combining multiple MA signals produces a factor that outperforms standard momentum
STreversal = return over past month (t-1). Jegadeesh (1990): stocks with high returns last month tend to reverse, earning lower returns next month. Driven by liquidity provision and overreaction
LRreversal = cumulative return from month t-60 to t-13. De Bondt and Thaler (1985): past losers over 3-5 years outperform past winners (reversal). Driven by mean-reversion and overreaction correction

CF = Cash Flow from Operations / Market Equity. Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny (1994): high cash-flow-to-price stocks earn higher returns. More robust value measure than B/M, less affected by accounting discretion
ROAQ = Quarterly Net Income / Total Assets. Balakrishnan, Bartov, Faurel (2010): quarterly ROA has incremental predictive power for future returns beyond annual measures due to timeliness

BetaFP = beta estimated using 1-day and 1-month overlapping returns with Dimson correction. Frazzini-Pedersen (2014) Betting Against Beta: low-beta stocks earn higher risk-adjusted returns than high-beta. BAB factor = leveraged low-beta minus de-leveraged high-beta

RealizedVol = standard deviation of daily returns over trailing month. Ang et al. (2006): total realized volatility negatively predicts future returns. Anomalous because higher risk should earn higher return per CAPM

Features synthesized by LLM with RAG from analyst estimates, options surfaces, and price-volume data. Over 500 unique features generated. Key types: (1) analyst revision momentum and dispersion, (2) implied volatility surface features, (3) put-call ratio signals, (4) price-volume microstructure. Ensemble Sharpe 1.14-1.63 net of costs. Low correlation (0.06-0.15) with traditional factors

Portfolio of stocks in the lowest decile of trailing realized volatility (std dev of daily returns over past 60-252 days). Low-volatility anomaly: low-vol stocks earn higher risk-adjusted returns than high-vol stocks. Explained by loading on different factor risks rather than being independent anomaly (AMF model)

factors.factor_name: Common Idiosyncratic Quantile (CIQ) Factor - Lower Tail
factors.definition: CIQ_lower = common factor extracted from lower quantiles (5th-25th percentile) of cross-sectional idiosyncratic return distributions using quantile factor analysis on rolling windows. After removing FF3 factors from returns, extract dominant factor of conditional lower-tail quantiles. High CIQ-beta stocks outperform low by 7-8% per year. Strengthens when intermediary capital is weak

factors.factor_name: Common Idiosyncratic Quantile (CIQ) Factor - Upper Tail
factors.definition: CIQ_upper = common factor extracted from upper quantiles (75th-95th percentile) of cross-sectional idiosyncratic return distributions. Captures common upside tail risk. Unlike lower-tail factor, upper-tail factor does not carry significant pricing premium

IdioVol adjusted for liquidity costs. Illiquidity-induced price bouncing inflates measured IdioVol. After correcting for bid-ask bounce and trading costs, the negative IdioVol-return relation weakens or disappears for liquid stocks. Adjusted IdioVol = raw IdioVol - liquidity noise component
factors.data_needed: daily_returns, bid_ask_spread, trading_volume, market_return, smb, hml

factors.definition: Systematic factor library of 101-158+ mathematically defined factors spanning: momentum (various lookbacks), reversal (short/long-term), volatility (realized, range-based), cross-sectional ranking patterns, volume-price interactions. Extended through parameter variations to 500-1000 factors. Processed through bias correction (industry/size neutralization) before ML model input

IC = Spearman rank correlation between factor values at time t and forward returns at t+1. Factor quality metric: IC_mean = average IC across time periods, IR = IC_mean / IC_std. After bias correction (neutralization), IC improves from 0.023 to 0.041 with positive IC rate from 54% to 68%
Mom6m = cumulative return from month t-7 to t-2 (or t-6 to t-1 excluding most recent). Jegadeesh and Titman (1993): 6-month momentum captures shorter-term continuation effect
BookLeverage = (Long-term Debt + Short-term Debt) / Total Assets. Fama and French (1992): book leverage is related to average returns. Higher leverage = higher financial risk
Cash = Cash and Short-term Investments / Total Assets. Palazzo (2012): cash holdings proxy for precautionary savings against future cash flow risk. Higher cash firms are safer
ShareVol = average daily shares traded / shares outstanding (trailing month). Datar, Naik, Radcliffe (1998): low turnover stocks earn higher returns, consistent with liquidity premium

MaxRet = maximum daily return within the past month. Bali, Cakici, Whitelaw (2011): stocks with extreme positive daily returns (lottery-like) earn lower subsequent returns. Captures lottery preference/speculation

BetaLiquidityPS = beta of stock return on Pastor-Stambaugh aggregate liquidity factor. Stocks with high liquidity beta (more sensitive to market liquidity shocks) earn higher returns as liquidity risk premium

NetEquityFinance = (Sale of Stock - Purchase of Stock) / Total Assets. Bradshaw, Richardson, Sloan (2006): firms issuing equity earn lower future returns (equity issuance anomaly). Net equity financing predicts negative returns

NetDebtFinance = (Issuance of Long-term Debt - Reduction of Long-term Debt) / Total Assets. Bradshaw, Richardson, Sloan (2006): net debt financing negatively predicts returns, complementary to equity issuance signal

ReturnSkew = third moment of daily return distribution over trailing month/quarter. Bali, Engle, Murray (2015): stocks with high positive skewness (lottery-like payoffs) earn lower average returns due to preference for positively skewed gambles

zerotrade = proportion of trading days with zero volume in the past month/quarter. Liu (2006): illiquidity measure that captures trading discontinuity. More zero-trade days = more illiquid = higher expected returns
DolVol = average daily price * volume over trailing month. Brennan, Chordia, Subrahmanyam (1998): stocks with lower trading volume earn higher returns, consistent with liquidity premium hypothesis
BidAskSpread = (Ask - Bid) / ((Ask + Bid)/2). Amihud and Mendelson (1986): wider spreads reflect higher transaction costs and illiquidity. Positive relation between spread and expected returns

CoskewACX = coskewness of stock returns with market returns using daily data. Ang, Chen, Xing (2006): stocks with more negative coskewness (tend to crash when market crashes) earn higher returns as compensation for downside risk

PriceDelayRsq = 1 - (R^2_restricted / R^2_unrestricted) from regressions of stock returns on contemporaneous and lagged market returns. Hou and Moskowitz (2005): high delay stocks respond slowly to market information, earn higher returns due to information friction

betaVIX = beta of stock return on changes in VIX (or equivalent volatility index). Ang et al. (2006): stocks with high sensitivity to aggregate volatility innovations earn lower returns. Volatility is priced risk factor with negative premium
AM = Total Assets / Market Equity. Fama and French (1992): alternative value measure. Similar to book-to-market but uses total assets instead of book equity, capturing both equity and debt financing

EquityDuration = Macaulay duration of expected equity cash flows. Dechow, Sloan, Soliman (2004): short-duration stocks (high current yield relative to growth) earn higher returns. Long-duration growth stocks are overpriced
CashProd = (Market Cap - Total Assets) / Cash. Chandrashekar and Rao (2009): measures how productively firms use cash holdings. Low cash productivity predicts higher future returns

Investment = Capital Expenditure / Revenue. Titman, Wei, Xie (2004): firms increasing investment relative to revenue earn lower subsequent returns, consistent with empire-building destroying shareholder value

MomSeason = average return in the same calendar month over years 2 to 5. Heston and Sadka (2008): stocks that performed well in a given month in prior years tend to perform well in the same month again. Calendar-based return predictability
factors.data_needed: monthly_returns (5 years history by calendar month)

factors.definition: Beta of a security relative to market portfolio. beta = Cov(r_i, r_m) / Var(r_m). Measures systematic risk exposure to the market factor.
Black (1972) zero-beta CAPM. E(r_i) - E(r_0m) = beta * [E(r_m) - E(r_0m)], where r_0m is the return on the zero-beta portfolio (minimum variance portfolio uncorrelated with market).
Implied growth rate from DDM: g = (P*r - D0) / (D + P). Or using P/E: g = (P/E0)*r / ((P/E0) + k), where k is payout ratio. Stocks with low implied growth are undervalued.
Ratio of earnings yield (E/P of S&P 500) to 10-year Treasury bond yield. When ratio > 1, market is undervalued; when < 1, overvalued. P/E1 = k / (r - (1-k)*ROE).
Harvey (2017): When too many investors adopt the same factor strategies, crowding compresses expected returns. Tests for multiple testing bias using t>3.0 threshold to declare significance.
Total Accruals = (delta_CA - delta_Cash) - (delta_CL - delta_STD - delta_TP) - DEP, scaled by average total assets. Long low accruals, short high accruals. Sloan (1996) original balance sheet method.

COMPACC = delta_CEQ - delta_CHE (change in common equity minus change in cash). Decomposes into: OPACC (operating accruals: change in non-cash operating assets minus change in operating liabilities) and FINACC (financial accruals: residual). Larson, Sloan & Giedt (2018).
WCACC = changes in short-term non-cash operating assets minus changes in short-term operating liabilities. Subset of OPACC focusing on current items only. Richardson et al. (2005) decomposition.

Changes in long-term non-cash operating assets minus changes in long-term operating liabilities. Includes capitalized software, PP&E, intangibles. Richardson et al. (2005) show less reliable accruals have lower earnings persistence.

Richardson et al. (2005): Rate accrual categories by reliability. Less reliable accruals (noncurrent operating, e.g. PP&E, intangibles) lead to lower earnings persistence and greater mispricing. Sort firms by reliability-weighted accrual measure.

Palmon et al. (2008): Double-sort on accruals and size. Positive abnormal returns concentrated in small firms with income-decreasing accruals; negative abnormal returns concentrated in large firms with income-increasing accruals.

Shi & Zhang: Two measures differ due to deferred taxes, equity in net earnings, gains/losses on PPE sales, other funds from operations, and non-articulations. Balance sheet accruals yield higher strategy returns than cash flow statement accruals.

Allen, Larson & Sloan (2009): Extreme accruals are followed by disproportionately high frequency of extreme reversals. These reversals explain the predictable earnings changes and stock returns following extreme accruals.

Leippold & Lohre (2012): Test accrual anomaly across 26 developed markets. After multiple testing correction (Romano-Wolf), robust only in US, Australia, Italy, Denmark. Anomaly diminishes over time as investors exploit it.

Bhojraj & Swaminathan (2009): Accrual anomaly extends to corporate bonds. High accrual firms' bonds underperform low accrual firms' bonds by 93-115 bps annually. Uses both WCA (working capital accruals) and NNI (net new investments including capex).

Richardson et al. (2005) broader accrual measure including capital investments. NNI = change in total non-cash assets minus change in total liabilities (excluding debt). Captures both working capital and long-term investment accruals.

Watanabe et al. (2012): Asset growth effect exists internationally — firms with higher asset growth rates have lower subsequent stock returns. Effect is stronger in more developed and efficiently priced markets. Consistent with optimal investment (q-theory) rather than mispricing.

Beaver, Kettler & Scholes (1970): Seven accounting risk measures associated with market beta: (1) dividend payout, (2) asset growth, (3) leverage, (4) liquidity, (5) asset size, (6) earnings variability, (7) accounting beta (covariance of firm earnings with market earnings).

Fong (2016): High-beta stocks (B5 quintile) earn significantly lower returns than low-beta stocks (B1). Over 20 years, $1 in B1 grows to $14.22 vs $6.26 in B5. Sharpe ratio B1=1.20 vs B5=0.48 at 10-year horizon. Effect worsens at longer horizons.

Chincarini, Kim & Moneta (2020): Beta declines over firm age. Decline persists for ~100 years. Driven by familiarity and estimation risk effects rather than fundamentals alone. Controlling for age, CAPM better explains cross-section of returns. Age-adjusted beta recommended for cost of capital.

Frazzini & Pedersen (2014): BAB factor = (1/beta_L)*(r_L - rf) - (1/beta_H)*(r_H - rf). Long leveraged low-beta assets, short de-leveraged high-beta assets, achieving zero market beta. US equity BAB Sharpe ratio = 0.78 (1926-2012). Works across 20 international equity markets, Treasuries, credit, futures. Driven by leverage constraints.

Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) beta estimation: beta_i = w * beta_TS + (1-w) * beta_XS, where beta_TS uses 1-year rolling daily stdev and 5-year rolling correlation (3-day overlapping returns), w=0.6, beta_XS=1. Shrinkage toward cross-sectional mean.

Black (1972): Zero-beta CAPM where investors cannot borrow at risk-free rate. Security market line is flatter than standard CAPM predicts. E(r_i) = E(r_z) + beta_i * [E(r_m) - E(r_z)] where r_z is zero-beta portfolio return > rf.

Black (1993): Empirical security market line is too flat — high-beta stocks earn less than CAPM predicts, low-beta stocks earn more. This persistent pattern challenges standard CAPM and supports restricted borrowing version.
Blume (1975): Measured betas tend to regress toward one over time. High betas decline, low betas increase. Adjustment formula: beta_adjusted = 0.371 + 0.635 * beta_raw (Merrill Lynch adjustment).
Blume (1971): Portfolio betas are more stable than individual stock betas. Larger portfolios have more stable betas. Beta estimation error decreases with portfolio size.

Thomas & Zhang (2002): Inventory changes have particularly strong negative association with future stock returns. Extremely positive inventory accruals are prone to extreme reversals and inventory write-downs.

Xie (2001): Mispricing is driven by abnormal (discretionary) accruals as measured by the Jones (1991) model. Abnormal accruals = total accruals minus predicted accruals from regression on revenue changes and PPE. Discretionary accruals reflect earnings management.
Lev & Nissim (2004): The accruals anomaly persists over time despite publication. Institutional investors partially exploit it but individual investors do not, explaining its persistence.

Bradshaw, Richardson & Sloan (2001): Analysts and auditors do not fully incorporate information in accruals. Analyst forecasts do not distinguish between accrual and cash flow components, contributing to accrual mispricing.

Richardson, Sloan, Soliman & Tuna (2006): Decompose implications of accounting distortions and growth for accruals and profitability. Growth in net operating assets drives lower future returns, subsuming traditional accrual measures.

Ali, Chen, Yao & Yu (2008): Examine whether mutual funds profit from accruals anomaly. Some mutual funds with higher accrual-based strategy exposure earn higher returns, but most do not fully exploit the anomaly.

Fu (2011): Decomposes asset growth and investment growth anomalies. Examines whether returns are driven by risk (q-theory optimal investment) or mispricing (overinvestment). Investment growth effect related to expected profitability changes.

Correlation of market order flow with the strength of the trading signal that factor investors follow. Measures crowding by looking at fluctuations of the imbalances of trades executed on the market. The actual holdings pi_i,t are given by an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the signal: pi_i,t = A * sum(s_i,t' * exp(-(t-t')/D)), and order flow is delta_pi_i,t = pi_i,t - pi_i,t-1.

Same cosine similarity crowding measure as crowding7 (s_ij = w_i'*w_j / (|w_i|*|w_j|)), applied to study how transaction cost models in portfolio construction affect crowding. Tests whether portfolios constructed with similar transaction cost models converge even when alpha models differ.

Crowded momentum trades identified via short interest. Loser stocks are split into crowded (high short interest) and non-crowded (low short interest) portfolios. Momentum crashes are driven by crowded losers experiencing short covering. Crowding proxy = short interest ratio of loser stocks.

Days-to-Cover = Short Ratio / Average Daily Share Turnover. A superior measure of binding short-sales constraints. Stocks with high DTC underperform the market by 140 basis points per month. Captures costliness of exiting crowded short positions.

Good-Minus-Poor (GMP) factor: portfolio long past winner funds, short past loser funds. A fund's GMP beta (loading on GMP factor over 12-month rolling window) measures crowdedness. Idiosyncratic winners (low GMP beta among past winners) outperform co-winners by 0.342% per month.

Actratio = (Percentage of shares held by active mutual funds at quarter t-2) / (Average share turnover during quarter t-1). High Actratio = crowded stock. Long least-crowded, short most-crowded decile generates DGTW-adjusted annualized return of 14.53%. More-crowded stocks earn lower future returns.

21-day mean pairwise correlation for a portfolio of stocks identified by a given trading strategy, compared to distribution of MPCs for 1,000 random portfolios. If strategy MPC exceeds random portfolio MPCs, the strategy is crowded. Referenced as Cahan and Luo (2013) measure.

Days-ADV = Hedge fund collective shareholdings / Average Daily Trading Volume. Measures how many days it would take hedge fund industry to exit collective position under typical volume. High crowdedness portfolios earn higher returns (Q5 11.3% vs Q1 8.5% annualized) but have higher tail risk during distress.

Classification of alternative risk premia into divergence (momentum-like, positive feedback loops, no fundamental anchor) and convergence (value-like, self-correction mechanism). Crowding measured by pairwise correlation of factor-adjusted returns of assets in the same peer group. Divergence premia underperform after crowded periods; convergence premia outperform.

Log growth in market equity minus log stock return over the prior five years. Captures net equity issuance including share repurchases, secondary offerings, and stock-based compensation. Daniel and Titman (2006).

NOA = (Total Assets - Cash) - (Total Assets - Short-term Debt - Long-term Debt - Minority Interest - Preferred Stock - Common Equity), scaled by lagged total assets. Hirshleifer, Hou, Teoh, and Zhang (2004). Cumulative accruals measure. Low NOA predicts higher returns.

Annual change in gross property, plant, and equipment plus annual change in inventories, scaled by lagged total assets. Titman, Wei, and Xie (2004); Xing (2008). Low investment firms outperform high investment firms.
Cumulative return over months t-12 to t-2 (skipping most recent month). Jegadeesh and Titman (1993); Carhart (1997). Long past winners, short past losers.

GP = (Revenue - COGS) / Total Assets. Novy-Marx (2013). High profitability firms outperform. Profitable firms generate significantly higher returns than unprofitable firms despite having higher valuation ratios.
ROA = Income before Extraordinary Items / Total Assets. Fama and French (2006); Wang and Yu (2010). Higher ROA predicts higher future returns.

Each month, rank stocks by percentile on each of nine anomaly variables, then average percentile ranks across anomalies to create composite mispricing measure. Stambaugh, Yu, Yuan (2015). Spread between top and bottom quintiles: cross-country average monthly alpha = 118 bps.

Book value of equity / Market value of equity. Captures excess returns to stocks with low prices relative to fundamental value. Also measured by earnings-to-price, sales-to-price, cash-flow-to-price, dividend yield.
Captures excess returns of smaller firms by market capitalization relative to larger counterparts. Fama and French (1993). SMB = Small minus Big portfolio return.

Captures excess returns to stocks with lower than average volatility, beta, and/or idiosyncratic risk. Measured by standard deviation (1-yr, 2-yrs, 3-yrs), downside standard deviation, idiosyncratic return volatility, or beta.
Captures excess returns to stocks with higher-than-average dividend yields. Dividend Yield = Annual Dividends / Price.

Captures excess returns to stocks characterized by low debt, stable earnings growth, and other quality metrics. Commonly measured by ROE, earnings stability, dividend growth stability, balance sheet strength, financial leverage, accounting policies, management quality, accruals, cash flows.

Implied IRR where initial outlay is cost to replicate asset base, annual cash flows are operating cash flows over asset life, and terminal value includes liquidation of non-depreciable assets. Tested as stock selection strategy on S&P 500; underperforms simpler ROA and ROC measures.

Return on a portfolio with zero covariance with the market portfolio. Black (1972) two-factor model: E(r_j) = E(r_z)(1-beta_j) + E(r_M)*beta_j. The zero-beta factor was ~1.0-1.3% per month (1948-65), significantly different from riskless rate.

First principal component of the covariance matrix of stock price changes. Represents market-wide effect of incoming information on all stocks. King (1966) found market factor explains ~31% of variance for typical stock, with the first factor looking like equally-weighted market.

Industry-specific component of stock price variation extracted via factor analysis. King (1966) found industry factors explain ~12% of variance for typical stock on top of market factor. Stocks grouped by industry show higher within-group correlations than cross-group.

Cross-sectional regression of stock returns on estimated betas each month. Tests whether beta explains cross-section of expected returns. Fama and MacBeth (1973) find positive risk-return tradeoff consistent with efficient market. E(R_i) = gamma_0 + gamma_1 * beta_i.

Standard deviation of residuals from Fama-French 3-factor model regression estimated using EGARCH. IVOL exhibits strong negative relation to alpha among overpriced stocks (arbitrage risk deters correction of overpricing). Positive correlation between IVOL and anomaly abnormal returns supports limits-of-arbitrage explanation.
Market capitalization of equity. Small firms earn higher risk-adjusted returns than large firms. Significant in 20 of 43 countries at 5% level.
Change in non-cash working capital minus depreciation, scaled by average total assets. Significant abnormal returns in 6 of 43 countries.
Annual change in total assets scaled by lagged total assets. Significant abnormal returns in 8 of 43 countries. Used as proxy for real investment anomaly.

Average predictor long-short return declines 26% out-of-sample and 58% post-publication across 97 variables. Decay is larger for predictors with higher in-sample returns, and lower for predictors concentrated in illiquid/high-IVOL stocks. McLean and Pontiff (2016).

231 anomalies tested across 39 stock markets. US shows 60% post-publication decline in equally-weighted anomaly returns. Non-US markets show NO reliable post-publication decline, suggesting limits to arbitrage or less quantitative arbitrage capital abroad. Jacobs and Mueller (2017).

452 anomaly variables replicated with NYSE breakpoints and value-weighted returns. 65% fail to clear |t|>=1.96; 82% fail |t|>=2.78 multiple-test hurdle. 96% of trading frictions category fail. Microcaps drive most published anomalies. Hou, Xue, Zhang (2020).

Aggregate hedge fund flows as proxy for smart money. Hedge fund flows attenuate cross-sectional mispricing (positive relation with Stambaugh-Yu-Yuan mispricing metric returns). Effect driven primarily by short positions in overvalued stocks.

Aggregate mutual fund flows as proxy for dumb money. Mutual fund flows exacerbate cross-sectional mispricing (negative contemporaneous relation with mispricing metric returns). Effect strongest for growth, accrual, and momentum anomalies. Mutual funds disproportionately purchase overvalued stocks.

Composite of 11 anomalies: each month identify stocks most likely overvalued/undervalued based on 11 characteristics. Return on hedge strategy long undervalued, short overvalued = time-varying metric of aggregate cross-sectional mispricing. Stambaugh, Yu, Yuan (2012, 2014).

Expected return of asset modeled as function of multiple macro/statistical factors: E(r_i) = r_f + beta_1*lambda_1 + ... + beta_k*lambda_k. Factors not pre-specified; discovered empirically. Ross (1976). Roll and Ross (1980) estimated principal components of covariance matrix to extract factors.

Three factors explain >96% of bond return cross-correlation: (1) Level - overall term structure level, >80% of bond return volatility; (2) Slope - spread between long and short ends, brings total to ~94%; (3) Curvature - convexity, butterfly portfolio, remaining ~2%.

Rosenberg's multi-factor risk model decomposing returns into company exposures to fundamentally-based factors ('risk indexes'). Original model had 39 factors including industry, size, beta, dividend yield, book-to-price, earnings yield, growth, leverage, volatility, momentum, etc. Predicts variance-covariance matrix from observable fundamentals.

Model selection method to evaluate new factor gt against high-dimensional set of existing factors ht. Two-stage LASSO: (1) select factors from ht with pricing ability; (2) add factors whose exposures correlate with gt exposures (to reduce omitted variable bias). Then test gt's SDF loading. Of 150 factors tested, most redundant; few (e.g. profitability) have significant marginal power.

Extra-market covariance component of security returns predicted by fundamental descriptors: industry, financial risk (leverage), growth orientation, size, earnings variability, success (momentum), trading activity. Rosenberg and Marathe (1976). Foundation for multi-factor risk models separating systematic from specific risk.

Standardized Unexpected Earnings = (Actual EPS - Expected EPS) / Std Dev of forecast errors. Post-earnings announcement drift: stocks with positive earnings surprises continue to outperform. Chan, Jegadeesh, Lakonishok (1996). Referenced in Hou, Xue, Zhang (2020) replication.

Operating accruals component of earnings. Sloan (1996). (Change in current assets - Change in cash) - (Change in current liabilities - Change in STD - Change in income taxes payable) - Depreciation, all scaled by average total assets. Significant even after HXZ replication controlling for microcaps.

Operating cash flow / Market capitalization. Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny (1994). Value stocks with high CF/P outperform growth stocks. Magnitude much lower than originally reported when microcaps controlled.
Cumulative return from month t-12 to t-2. Jegadeesh-Titman (1993). Significant in replication but magnitude much lower than originally reported. Long winners, short losers.
Average daily trading volume / shares outstanding. Datar, Naik, Radcliffe (1998). Fails to replicate with microcaps controlled.

Standard deviation of daily residuals from FF3 model over past month. Ang, Hodrick, Xing, Zhang (2006). Originally high IVOL stocks have low future returns. Fails to replicate with microcaps controlled.
Standard deviation of analyst EPS forecasts / absolute value of mean forecast. Diether, Malloy, Scherbina (2002). High dispersion predicts lower future returns. Insignificant in HXZ replication.
Change in consensus analyst EPS forecast. Chan, Jegadeesh, Lakonishok (1996). Positive revisions predict higher future returns. Survives as significant anomaly in replication.

Average same-calendar-month return over prior years. Heston and Sadka (2008). Has significant alpha vs FF3 (t=2.06) but becomes insignificant when momentum is included as control (correlation 0.63 with momentum factor).

Operating income / Book equity. Fama and French (2015) profitability factor. Insignificant in HXZ replication using NYSE breakpoints and VW returns, but significant in Feng-Giglio-Xiu (2020) double-selection LASSO test.
Total debt / Market equity. Bhandari (1988). High leverage firms earn higher returns. Insignificant in HXZ replication.
Cash-based operating profits / Total assets. Survives HXZ replication as significant anomaly even after q-factor model adjustment. One of the few robust profitability measures.
R&D expenditure / Market capitalization. High R&D intensity firms earn higher future returns. Survives as significant anomaly in HXZ replication even after q-factor model.

Cumulative abnormal return in 3-day window around earnings announcement. Chan, Jegadeesh, Lakonishok (1996). Positive CAR predicts positive drift. Survives as significant anomaly even in HXZ replication.

Average daily ratio of absolute stock return to dollar trading volume: ILLIQ_iy = (1/D_iy) * sum(|R_iyd| / VOLD_iyd) over all days d in year y, where D_iy is the number of trading days with data, R_iyd is the return on stock i on day d of year y, and VOLD_iyd is the dollar volume. Multiplied by 10^6 for scaling. Mean-adjusted version: ILLIQMA_iy = ILLIQ_iy / AILLIQ_y where AILLIQ_y is the cross-sectional average.

Modified version of Amihud (2002) that uses absolute open-to-close return instead of close-to-close return in the numerator: OCAM = (1/D) * sum(|OCR_id| / VOLD_id), where OCR_id is the open-to-close return on day d. This removes overnight returns from the numerator, correcting the time mismatch between returns (which include overnight) and volume (which covers only regular trading hours). Produces 50-120% larger estimates of liquidity premia compared to original CCAM.

Cross-sectional average of individual stock ILLIQ measures: AILLIQ_y = (1/N_y) * sum(ILLIQ_iy) over all N_y stocks in year y. Used as aggregate market illiquidity measure. Expected market illiquidity positively affects ex ante stock excess return; unexpected illiquidity negatively affects contemporaneous returns.

Relative bid-ask spread = (Ask - Bid) / Midpoint. Average of beginning- and end-of-year relative spreads used as proxy for liquidity. Market-observed expected return is an increasing and concave function of the relative spread. Higher-spread assets yield higher expected returns with a clientele effect: investors with longer holding periods select higher-spread assets.

For each stock i in month t, estimate gamma_i,t from the regression: r^e_{i,d+1,t} = theta_{i,t} + phi_{i,t} * r_{i,d,t} + gamma_{i,t} * sign(r^e_{i,d,t}) * v_{i,d,t} + epsilon_{i,d+1,t}, where r^e_{i,d,t} = r_{i,d,t} - r_{m,d,t} is stock excess return over market, v_{i,d,t} is dollar volume in millions. Gamma captures the strength of volume-related return reversals. Lower (more negative) gamma = lower liquidity. Aggregate liquidity = equal-weighted average of individual gammas across eligible NYSE/AMEX stocks.

Innovations L_t to aggregate liquidity computed as residuals from: Delta_gamma_hat_t = a + b * Delta_gamma_hat_{t-1} + c * (m_{t-1}/m_t) * gamma_hat_{t-1} + 100*L_t, where Delta_gamma_hat_t = (m_t/m_1) * (1/N_t) * sum(gamma_i,t - gamma_i,t-1) is scaled changes in average liquidity, m_t is market capitalization of eligible stocks. L_t captures unexpected changes in marketwide liquidity.

Long-short portfolio based on liquidity betas. Each year, sort stocks by predicted liquidity betas (from regression r_i = alpha + beta_L * L_t + beta_M * MKT + beta_S * SMB + beta_H * HML + epsilon) into deciles. Factor = return on top decile (high liquidity beta) minus bottom decile (low liquidity beta). Rebalanced annually at end of December. 7.5% annual alpha (1966-1999) adjusted for market, size, value, and momentum.

Net beta decomposes into standard market beta plus three liquidity betas: (1) Commonality in liquidity: cov(c_i, c_M) - covariance of stock illiquidity cost with market illiquidity cost; (2) Return sensitivity to market liquidity: cov(r_i, c_M) - covariance of stock return with market illiquidity; (3) Liquidity sensitivity to market returns: cov(c_i, r_M) - covariance of stock illiquidity with market return. Uses Amihud ILLIQ as proxy for c_i. Expected return = rf + E(c_i) + lambda * net_beta.

Per-share cost of selling security i, modeled as autoregressive process: C_t = C_bar + rho_C * (C_{t-1} - C_bar) + eta_t. Proxied empirically by Amihud (2002) ILLIQ measure. Persistent negative shock to liquidity results in low contemporaneous returns and high predicted future returns.

factors.factor_name: Kyle Lambda (Price Impact / Market Depth Inverse)
factors.definition: From Kyle (1985) continuous auction model: lambda measures the price impact per unit of order flow. In the Glosten-Harris estimation: Delta_p_t = lambda * q_t + psi * (D_t - D_{t-1}) + y_t, where q_t is signed trade quantity, D_t is trade direction indicator. Lambda represents the inverse of market depth - the variable (information-driven) component of trading costs. Higher lambda = more illiquid.

Fixed (non-information) component of proportional trading cost, estimated from Glosten-Harris model: Delta_p_t = lambda * q_t + psi * (D_t - D_{t-1}) + y_t. Psi captures the fixed-cost component related to bid-ask spread, independent of trade size. Both lambda and psi are positively related to expected stock returns after controlling for Fama-French three factors.

Price response to unexpected order flow. Estimate two-equation system: (1) q_t = alpha_q + sum(beta_j * dp_{t-j}) + sum(gamma_j * q_{t-j}) + z_t (order flow equation with 5 lags); (2) Delta_p_t = alpha_p + psi * (D_t - D_{t-1}) + lambda * z_t + v_t. Lambda coefficient on residual z_t from first equation measures trade informativeness - the price response to unexpected component of order flow.

Standardized turnover-adjusted number of zero daily trading volumes over prior x months: LM_x = [Number of zero daily volumes in prior x months + (1/(x-month turnover))/Deflator] * (21x/NoTD), where x-month turnover is sum of daily turnover ratios, NoTD is total trading days, Deflator ensures the turnover adjustment is between 0 and 1. LM12 (x=12) is primary measure. Captures trading speed (continuity of trading), trading quantity (via turnover adjustment), and trading cost dimensions.

Mimicking liquidity factor constructed as: LIQ = return on low-liquidity portfolio minus return on high-liquidity portfolio, where stocks are sorted into deciles by LM12. Buy $1 of least liquid decile, sell $1 of most liquid decile. Used in two-factor model: E(r_i) - r_f = beta_M * [E(r_M) - r_f] + beta_LIQ * E(LIQ). This two-factor model subsumes size, book-to-market, cash-flow-to-price, earnings-to-price, dividend yield, and long-term contrarian anomalies.

Number of shares traded divided by number of shares outstanding, averaged over prior 3 months. Turnover_it = avg(monthly_volume_{t-3 to t-1}) / shares_outstanding_i. Stocks with lower turnover (less liquid) earn higher returns. Negative cross-sectional relationship with returns persists after controlling for size, book-to-market, and beta. Theoretically linked to Amihud-Mendelson model: proportional to holding period frequency parameter k.

Annual share turnover = sum of 12 monthly volumes divided by each month's shares outstanding. Used to sort stocks into quartiles. Low-turnover (Q1) stocks outperform high-turnover (Q4) stocks: geometric mean 14.50% vs 7.24% annually (1972-2011). Low-liquidity quartile has highest return with lowest risk (std dev 20.41% vs 28.48%). Liquidity proposed as 5th investment style alongside size, value, and momentum.

From tick-by-tick TAQ data, decompose price impact into four components: permanent-fixed, transitory-fixed, permanent-variable, and transitory-variable. Aggregate firm-level estimates into monthly market-wide measures. Apply AR(3) to generate uncorrelated innovation shocks. Only the permanent-variable component is priced in cross-section. Sign reversed so positive shock = liquidity improvement. Funds loading on this factor earn ~6% annual premium.

Illiquidity measure = (sigma^2 / (P * V))^(1/3), the cube root of the ratio of returns variance to dollar volume. Bid-ask spread is proportional to this measure. Market impact formula: G ~ (sigma^2 / (P*V))^(1/3) * f((sigma^2/(P*V))^(1/3) * |P*Q|), where Q is bet size, V is share volume, sigma^2 is returns variance, P is stock price. Nests both square-root (beta=1/2) and linear (beta=1) impact models.

Basic liquidity measure proportional to the cube root of ratio of dollar volume to return variance: L ~ (P*V / sigma^2)^(1/3). Bid-ask spreads inversely proportional to this measure. Trade arrival rate proportional to L^2 * sigma^2. Derived from dimensional analysis + leverage neutrality + market microstructure invariance. Scaling laws: bid-ask spread ~ L^(-1), number of trades ~ L^2 * sigma^2.

G = sigma * (|Q|/V)^(1/2), where G is percentage cost of executing a bet of Q shares, sigma is daily returns standard deviation, V is daily share volume. Proportionality constant approximately equals 1. Example: if daily volatility is 2% and trading 5% of daily volume, market impact is about 0.02*(0.05)^0.5 = 45 basis points. Dimensionally consistent and empirically realistic.

Equilibrium gross return on asset j: d_j/V_j* = min over investor types i of (r_i* + mu_i * S_j), where d_j is cash flow, V_j* is equilibrium price, r_i* is spread-adjusted return for investor type i, mu_i is liquidation probability, S_j is relative spread. Market-observed expected return is increasing and concave piecewise-linear function of the relative bid-ask spread. Clientele effect: higher-spread assets allocated to longer holding period investors.

For asset j and investor type i: r_ij = d_j/V_j - mu_i * S_j, where d_j/V_j is gross market return on asset j, and mu_i * S_j is expected liquidation cost per unit time (product of liquidation probability mu_i and percentage spread S_j). The spread-adjusted return depends on both asset characteristics and investor type (through holding period). Returns net of trading costs increase with holding period.

Daily or monthly dollar trading volume = price * shares traded. Brennan, Chordia, and Subrahmanyam (1998) find dollar volume has a significant negative effect on cross-section of stock returns, subsuming the negative size effect. Higher dollar volume = more liquid = lower expected returns.

Ratio of sum of daily dollar volumes to sum of absolute daily returns: LR = sum(VOLD_d) / sum(|R_d|). Inverse of Amihud ILLIQ in aggregate form. Higher values indicate more liquid stocks. Used by Cooper et al. (1985), Khan and Baker (1993), Amihud et al. (1997), Berkman and Eleswarapu (1998) to study effects of liquidity changes on stock values.

Absolute difference between the mid-point of the quoted bid-ask spread and the transaction price, classified as buy or sell. Amortized version: effective spread divided by stock's holding period (obtained from turnover ratio). Higher effective spread = more illiquid = higher expected returns. From Hasbrouck (2009) estimation method.

Slope coefficient beta_L from regression: r_{i,t} = alpha_i + beta_L_i * L_t + beta_M_i * MKT_t + beta_S_i * SMB_t + beta_H_i * HML_t + epsilon_{i,t}, where L_t is the Pastor-Stambaugh liquidity innovation factor. Stocks with higher liquidity betas (more sensitive to aggregate liquidity drops) earn higher expected returns. Can be predicted using historical beta plus stock characteristics.

Beta measuring covariation of individual stock illiquidity with market-wide illiquidity: cov(c_i, c_M). From Acharya-Pedersen model. Contributes approximately 0.08% annual return premium. Captures whether a stock becomes illiquid when the overall market becomes illiquid.

Beta measuring covariation of stock return with market illiquidity: cov(r_i, c_M). From Acharya-Pedersen model. Contributes approximately 0.16% annual return premium. Investors prefer securities with high returns when the market is illiquid.

Beta measuring covariation of stock illiquidity with market return: cov(c_i, r_M). From Acharya-Pedersen model. Largest liquidity risk component at approximately 0.82% annual return premium. Investors pay premium for stocks that are liquid when market returns are low (flight to liquidity).

factors.factor_name: Proportion of Zero Returns (Emerging Market Liquidity)
factors.definition: Fraction of trading days with zero daily firm returns over a given period. Used as liquidity proxy especially in emerging markets where volume data may be unavailable. From Bekaert, Harvey, and Lundblad (2007). Zero returns may indicate absence of trading (illiquidity). Problematic if returns are based on price quotes rather than transaction prices.

Li, Mooradian, and Zhang (2007) examine whether illiquidity measured by commission costs is a risk factor. Commission costs can be expressed as either a metric (stock characteristic) or a risk factor (covariance-based). Distinguishes between liquidity level and liquidity risk.

Covariation of hedge fund monthly returns with unexpected changes in aggregate liquidity (Sadka permanent-variable component). Sort funds by liquidity loading into quintiles. High-loading minus low-loading portfolio earns ~6% annually (1994-2008). Independent of fund-level liquidity (lockup/redemption periods). Underperforms during liquidity crises (LTCM 1998, Quant crisis 2007, Financial crisis 2008).

Product of dollar volume and returns volatility: W = P * V * sigma. Under market microstructure invariance, the number of bets per calendar day is proportional to W^(2/3). Average bet size (as fraction of volume) is inversely proportional to W^(2/3). Trading activity determines the speed of business time relative to calendar time.

Second moment (variability/coefficient of variation) of liquidity proxied by trading activity measures such as dollar volume and turnover. Chordia, Subrahmanyam, and Anshuman (2001) find that stocks with more volatile liquidity have LOWER expected returns (counterintuitive result). Distinguishes firm-specific liquidity variability from systematic liquidity risk.

Illiquidity measure derived from Kyle (1985) theory incorporating return volatility and volume: incorporates parameters such as return volatility and volume into the illiquidity measure as indicated by Kyle's expression for illiquidity in equilibrium. Positively related to future expected returns. From Chordia, Subrahmanyam et al. (2008).

Differential price impact on sell-side vs buy-side of trades. Brennan et al. (2008) show that sell-side price impact is the component actually priced in cross-section of expected returns. Demands for immediacy are greater on sell-side (unanticipated liquidity needs force selling more than buying), strengthening the premium for sell-side illiquidity.

Sort stocks by estimated market beta (from regression of stock returns on market returns, typically 60 months). Long low-beta stocks, short high-beta stocks. The security market line is flatter than CAPM predicts - low-beta stocks outperform on risk-adjusted basis.

factors.factor_name: Aggregate Volatility Risk (Sensitivity to VIX innovations)
factors.definition: Stocks with high sensitivity to innovations in aggregate market volatility have low average returns. Measured by regressing individual stock returns on changes in VIX or realized market volatility. Idiosyncratic volatility relative to FF3 model also negatively predicts returns.

Optimize portfolio weights to minimize total portfolio variance: min w'*Sigma*w, subject to sum(w)=1 and constraints (max weight per stock, sector bounds, turnover limits). Uses Barra multi-factor covariance matrix for estimation. The MSCI Min Vol methodology.

factors.factor_name: Benchmarks as Limits to Arbitrage (Low-Vol Anomaly Explanation)
factors.definition: The low-volatility anomaly persists because institutional investors with fixed benchmark mandates cannot exploit it - buying low-beta stocks creates tracking error vs cap-weighted benchmarks. Lottery preference and overconfidence drive demand for high-vol stocks. Sort stocks into volatility deciles using trailing 60-month volatility. Baker, Bradley, Wurgler (2011).

Weight each stock (or asset) inversely proportional to its volatility (or proportional to 1/sigma_i), so each contributes equally to total portfolio risk. w_i = (1/sigma_i) / sum(1/sigma_j). A systematic approach to low-risk investing.

Sort stocks cross-sectionally by trailing total return volatility (e.g., 12-month realized vol). Low-volatility quintile outperforms high-volatility quintile both in raw returns and risk-adjusted returns. Distinct from time-series vol anomaly. De Jong and Palkar.

Quality = z-score composite of Profitability + Growth + Safety. Profitability = z(GPOA, ROE, ROA, CFOA, GMAR, ACC). Growth = z(5-year growth of profitability measures). Safety = z(low_beta, low_vol, low_leverage, low_bankruptcy_risk). QMJ = Long high-quality, short low-quality (junk) stocks. Asness, Frazzini, Pedersen (2019).
CFOA = Operating Cash Flow / Total Assets. A profitability measure used in QMJ factor construction. High CFOA indicates quality earnings backed by real cash generation.

ACC = (Net Income - Operating Cash Flow) / Total Assets. Low accruals (i.e., high cash component of earnings) indicate higher quality earnings. Used as input to QMJ profitability score (reversed sign: low accruals = high quality).

factors.factor_name: Safety (Low Leverage, Low Beta, Low Vol)
factors.definition: Safety z-score = z(low_market_beta, low_idiosyncratic_vol, low_leverage, low_bankruptcy_risk, low_earnings_vol). Component of QMJ. Low leverage = low total debt / total assets. Firms that are safe (low financial risk) tend to have higher risk-adjusted returns.

R_i - R_f = alpha + b*(R_m - R_f) + s*SMB + h*HML + r*RMW + c*CMA + epsilon. SMB = Small Minus Big (size), HML = High Minus Low (value, B/M), RMW = Robust Minus Weak (operating profitability), CMA = Conservative Minus Aggressive (investment). Fama and French (2015).

factors.factor_name: RMW (Robust Minus Weak - Operating Profitability Factor)
factors.definition: RMW = average return of robust profitability portfolios minus average return of weak profitability portfolios. Operating profitability = (Revenue - COGS - SGA - Interest Expense) / Book Equity. Constructed using 2x3 independent sorts on size and operating profitability. Fama and French (2015).

CMA = average return of conservative investment portfolios minus average return of aggressive investment portfolios. Investment = total asset growth rate: (Total_Assets_t - Total_Assets_{t-1}) / Total_Assets_{t-1}. Constructed using 2x3 independent sorts on size and investment. Fama and French (2015).

factors.factor_name: Choosing Factors: Max Squared Sharpe Ratio
factors.definition: Compare nested and non-nested factor models using maximum squared Sharpe ratio of model factors as metric. Cash profitability vs operating profitability, long-short spread factors vs excess return factors. The six-factor model adds momentum to FF5. Fama and French (2018).

Cash profitability = (Revenue - COGS - SGA - Interest - Accruals) / Book Equity. Differs from operating profitability by subtracting accruals. Examined as alternative to operating profitability in FF factor model. Fama and French (2018) 'Choosing Factors'.

Gross Profits-to-Assets = (Revenue - COGS) / Total Assets. Profitable firms generate significantly higher returns than unprofitable firms, despite having higher valuation ratios. Complementary to value (B/M). Controlling for profitability dramatically increases performance of value strategies. Novy-Marx (2013).

Cross-sectional return predictive power is stronger when profit is measured by gross profit and scaled by enterprise value (EV) or market value of equity (ME) rather than total assets. GP/EV = Gross Profit / Enterprise Value. GP/ME = Gross Profit / Market Equity. Cakici, Chatterjee, Tang, Tong.

Profitability anomaly arises from investors' sticky expectations - they update beliefs too slowly about persistent profitability signals (e.g., operating cash flows to assets). Sort stocks on trailing operating profitability; high-profitability outperforms. Anomaly is stronger for firms with more persistent earnings and stickier analyst forecasts.

RMW (profitability factor) and HML (value) improve mean-variance efficient tangency portfolio in pre-1963 hand-collected data. CMA (investment factor) does NOT reliably predict returns pre-1963. Profitability measured as operating profitability. Investment measured as total asset growth or book equity growth. Wahal (2019).

P = D / (k - g), where P = stock price, D = expected dividend per share, k = required rate of return (discount rate), g = constant growth rate of dividends. Equivalently: k = D/P + g. Higher dividend yield or lower price relative to dividends implies higher expected return. Gordon (1962).

Higher dividends are associated with higher future earnings growth, contradicting the common view that high dividends signal low growth. Firms paying higher dividends tend to have higher subsequent earnings growth because reinvestment at low rates destroys value. Arnott and Asness (2003) FAJ.
factors.source_paper: Surprise Higher Dividends Equal Higher Earnings Growth.pdf

factors.definition: HML = High Minus Low book-to-market ratio. Long stocks with high B/M (value), short stocks with low B/M (growth). Value premium is the excess return of value stocks over growth stocks. Updated evidence through 2019 shows value premium has weakened but not disappeared.

E(R_i) = R_f + beta_i * [E(R_m) - R_f]. The expected return of a security equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Beta = Cov(R_i, R_m) / Var(R_m). Sharpe (1964), Lintner (1965), Mossin (1966).

Select portfolios that maximize expected return for a given level of variance, or minimize variance for given expected return. The efficient frontier is the set of all such optimal portfolios. Portfolio variance = w'*Sigma*w, expected return = w'*mu. Markowitz (1952).

E(R_i) = R_f + b_i1*lambda_1 + b_i2*lambda_2 + ... + b_ik*lambda_k. Returns are generated by a linear factor model: R_i = a_i + b_i1*F_1 + ... + b_ik*F_k + epsilon_i. No-arbitrage implies expected returns are linear in factor loadings. Ross (1976).

Equilibrium in a market for risky assets where investors maximize expected utility (mean-variance preferences). In equilibrium, each investor holds a combination of the market portfolio and the risk-free asset. Pricing kernel implies linear risk-return relation. Mossin (1966).

First formulation of CAPM. Expected excess return of a security is proportional to its systematic risk (beta). The 'characteristic line' relates security return to market return. Treynor (1961/1962, unpublished manuscript).

Extension of CAPM allowing heterogeneous investor expectations. Security valuation depends on expected returns, variances, and covariances as perceived by the market. Equilibrium risk premium is proportional to the security's covariance with the market portfolio. Lintner (1965).

Four-factor model: R_i - R_f = alpha + b*(R_m-R_f) + s*SMB + h*HML + p*PR1YR + e. PR1YR (or UMD/WML) = one-year momentum factor = return of top 30% past 12-month winners minus bottom 30% past 12-month losers (skip most recent month). Explains persistence in mutual fund performance. Carhart (1997).
factors.source_paper: The Journal of Finance - 2012 - Carhart - On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance.pdf

factors.definition: Gen-1 Value: Select stocks with low P/E, P/B, or P/S ratios from a broad universe, weight by market cap or equal weight within value universe. Concentrated Value: More concentrated tilt toward deepest value stocks. RAFI Value Factor: value tilt using fundamental weights.

Select stocks with high quality characteristics: stable sales growth, stable earnings growth, low leverage, high ROE/ROA. Variants include sector-neutral quality, growth-and-stability combination, RAFI Quality Factor. Often combined with value and low-vol for multi-factor.

factors.factor_name: Smart Beta Minimum Volatility / Low Volatility
factors.definition: Minimum Volatility: optimization-based approach minimizing portfolio volatility with constraints. Low Volatility: rank-and-select approach selecting lowest volatility stocks and weighting inversely by vol. Defensive: broader definition including low beta and quality screens. RAFI LV Factor: fundamental weight + vol tilt.

Combine multiple factor tilts in a single portfolio. Mathematical Beta 4: combine value, quality, momentum, low-vol. Mathematical Beta 6: add size and dividend. Quality/Value/Low Vol: triple tilt. RAFI Dynamic Multi-Factor: dynamically allocate across factors based on valuations.

factors.factor_name: Smart Beta Size (Small Cap / Equal Weight / Fundamental Size)
factors.definition: Small Cap: select stocks below median market cap. Equal Weight: weight all constituents equally (tilts toward small). Equal Sector Equal Weight: equal weight within each sector. RAFI Fundamental Size Factor: size measured by sales, dividends, book value, cash flow instead of market cap.

Weight stocks by composite fundamental size: average of (sales, cash flow, book value, dividends) relative to universe total, rather than market capitalization. Arnott, Hsu, Moore (2005). Fundamentally-weighted indices outperform cap-weighted benchmarks on risk-adjusted basis.

Heuristic weighting alternatives to cap-weighting: Equal Weight (1/N), Diversity Weighted, Inverse Volatility, Maximum Diversification. All outperform cap-weighted on risk-adjusted basis. Even random (monkey) portfolios outperform cap-weighted. Amenc, Goltz, Lodh; Clare et al.

Maximize the diversification ratio: DR = w'*sigma / sqrt(w'*Sigma*w), where sigma is the vector of individual volatilities and Sigma is the covariance matrix. This maximizes the ratio of weighted-average volatility to portfolio volatility.

For each smart beta factor, capacity = AUM level where transaction costs from flows negate the smart beta premium. At 1-day trading horizon: Momentum ~$50B, Size ~$3T, Value/Quality/MinVol in between. At 5-day horizon, capacity rises to ~$320B (momentum) and >$10T (size). Ang, Ratcliffe, Miranda (BlackRock).

Smart beta index returns drop from ~3.4% per year 'on paper' before ETF listing to ~0.5% per year after ETF listing. Performance deterioration driven by data mining in constructing smart beta indexes rather than crowding or time trends in factor premia. Huang, Song, Xiang (2020).

Growing popularity of smart beta strategies may lead to crowding, where flows into factor strategies inflate factor valuations and compress future expected returns. Herding behavior in smart beta products documented across momentum, value, quality, and low-vol factors. Krkoska, Schenk-Hoppe (2020).

factors.factor_name: Strategic Beta on Style Portfolios (Diversification Return)
factors.definition: Apply strategic beta (non-cap-weighted) allocation to investment style portfolios (sorted by size, value, momentum) rather than individual stocks. Dependent sorting (controlling for correlated variables) delivers significantly higher Sharpe ratios than independent sorting. Fays, Lambert, Papageorgiou (2017).

Time factor tilts based on relative valuations of factor portfolios vs history. When a factor portfolio is cheap relative to its historical average, increase tilt. Arnott et al. (2016) argue that much of smart beta's historical excess return comes from increasing valuations (getting more expensive) rather than alpha. Mean reversion of factor valuations suggests timing can add value.

factors.factor_name: Smart Beta Value Trap (Structural Alpha vs Revaluation)
factors.definition: Decompose smart beta returns into structural alpha (genuine factor premium) and revaluation alpha (rising valuations of factor portfolios). If a factor strategy has become more expensive (lower yields), past returns overstate future expected returns. Arnott et al. (2016) 'How Can Smart Beta Go Horribly Wrong'.
factors.source_paper: Fundamentals.2016 02.Arnott et al.How Can Smart Beta Go Horribly Wrong.pdf

factors.definition: Exponentially weighted moving average of factor index active return (factor index return minus market return). Computed over window lengths of 8, 21, 63 trading days.

factors.factor_name: Relative Strength Index (RSI) on Factor Active Returns
factors.definition: RSI computed on factor active returns over window lengths of 8, 21, 63 trading days. Measures overbought/oversold conditions of factor relative performance.

factors.factor_name: Stochastic Oscillator %K on Factor Active Returns
factors.definition: Stochastic oscillator %K computed on factor active returns using rolling window lengths of 8, 21, 63 trading days.
Moving Average Convergence/Divergence computed on factor active returns with short/long window pairs of (8,21) and (21,63) trading days.

factors.factor_name: Downside Deviation of Factor Active Returns
factors.definition: Log of exponentially weighted downside deviation (focusing on negative active returns) with 21-day window. Measures factor-specific downside risk.
Exponentially weighted beta of factor active returns against market returns with 21-day window. Measures factor's sensitivity to broad market.
Exponentially weighted moving average of broad market returns with 21-day window. Market-environment feature for regime detection.
EWMA of log-returns of VIX index with 21-day window. Positive values indicate increasing volatility environment, negative values decreasing.
EWMA of daily differences in 2-year Treasury yield with 21-day window. Captures monetary policy direction.
EWMA of daily differences in 10Y minus 2Y Treasury yield spread with 21-day window. Captures yield curve flattening/steepening trends.

Sparse Jump Model (SJM) identifies bull/bear regimes for individual style factors (value, size, momentum, quality, low volatility, growth) using factor-specific and market-environment features. Enhances regime persistence via jump penalty at each state transition. Online inference via Bayesian update of regime probabilities.

Modified k-means clustering on 100+ monthly macroeconomic time series from FRED-MD database. Two-step approach: (1) L2-distance k-means with k=2 to separate outlier months (Regime 0) from typical months, (2) cosine-distance clustering on typical months to identify distinct macro regimes. Produces fuzzy membership probabilities across regimes.

Expected asset return conditional on the most likely predicted next-period macro regime. Computed as the sample mean of historical returns occurring during the same regime classification. Used as view input to Black-Litterman model.
Sharpe ratio of each asset computed only using return observations from time steps matching the predicted next-period regime. Used for naive forecasting model asset ranking.

Three-state volatility regime classifier using CBOE VIX. Regime thresholds are 33rd and 67th percentiles of trailing 252-day VIX distribution. Low regime: VIX <= Q33, Medium: Q33 < VIX <= Q67, High: VIX > Q67. Each day assigned to one of three regimes conditioning downstream forecasting and allocation.
Standard RSI technical indicator computed on stock price. Used as predictive feature in regime-aware ensemble models.
Standard MACD technical indicator. Used as predictive feature within regime-specific sector ensemble models.
Bollinger Bands technical indicator (mean +/- k standard deviations of rolling price). Used as predictive feature for regime-aware models.
Rolling standard deviation of returns. Used as predictive feature in regime-specific ensemble models.
Price momentum computed over 5, 10, and 20-day horizons. Used as predictive feature in regime-aware portfolio optimization.
ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread. Captures aggregate credit risk as macroeconomic factor for regime-aware models.

Weighted momentum score: (12 * (p0/p1 - 1)) + (4 * (p0/p3 - 1)) + (2 * (p0/p6 - 1)) + (p0/p12 - 1), where p0=current month-end price, p1=1 month ago, p3=3 months ago, p6=6 months ago, p12=12 months ago. Heavily overweights recent months (1-month change = 40% of score). Used for both relative and absolute momentum decisions.

Fraction of assets in offensive universe with positive momentum scores. When all offensive assets have positive momentum, allocate offensively; when any have negative momentum, switch to defensive assets. Uses market breadth to determine crash protection allocation.

Separate 'canary' universe of leading indicator assets (e.g., EEM, AGG) used to signal crash protection need. If any canary asset shows negative momentum score, entire portfolio switches to defensive allocation. Inspired by 'canaries in coal mines' concept.

Combines traditional dual momentum (absolute + relative) with 'dimmed' canary momentum signal. Canary signal is softened to make dual momentum more useful for crash protection. Designed for rising yield/inflation environments.

Momentum score MOM_t = (close_t / SMA(t..t-12)) - 1, where SMA is 13-month simple moving average. Number of assets with positive momentum determines defensive allocation ratio via breadth protection formula.

50/50 combination of (1) 1-year change in real GDP growth forecasts and (2) 1-year change in CPI inflation forecasts. Increasing growth is bullish for equities/currencies, bearish for bonds. Increasing inflation is bearish for equities, bullish for currencies.
factors.source_paper: A Half Century of Macro Momentum(2017).pdf

factors.definition: 1-year change in spot FX rate measured against an export-weighted basket. FX depreciation = increasing competitiveness, bullish for equities.
factors.source_paper: A Half Century of Macro Momentum(2017).pdf

factors.definition: 1-year change in 2-year government bond yield. Rising yields indicate policy tightening, bearish for equities and bonds.
factors.source_paper: A Half Century of Macro Momentum(2017).pdf

factors.definition: 1-year equity market return as proxy for risk sentiment. Positive return = improving risk sentiment, bullish for equities and currencies, bearish for bonds.
factors.source_paper: A Half Century of Macro Momentum(2017).pdf

factors.definition: Binary regime indicator: inflationary regime defined as period when YoY realized CPI inflation rises materially beyond 2%, reaching 5% or more. Regime end defined when CPI YoY reaches peak without falling below 50% of peak. Eight historical US inflationary regimes identified since 1926.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times(2020).pdf

factors.definition: Time-series momentum across equities, bonds, commodities, and currencies. Positive trend = long, negative trend = short. Bonds and commodities trend performs especially well during inflationary periods.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times(2020).pdf

factors.definition: Standard long-short equity momentum factor. Historically earns +8% real annualized return during inflationary regimes with 75% hit rate across eight episodes, though results are regime-dating-sensitive.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times(2020).pdf

factors.definition: Quality factor as formulated by Asness, Frazzini, and Pedersen (2019). Holds up well during inflationary periods, providing inflation-robust returns.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times(2020).pdf

factors.definition: Low-beta factor as formulated by Frazzini and Pedersen (2014). Long low-beta stocks, short high-beta stocks. Performance during inflationary regimes analyzed.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times(2020).pdf

factors.definition: Risk parity combined with time-series momentum across global asset classes (equities, bonds, commodities, currencies). Position sizing via trend-following signals. Equal risk contribution with momentum overlay.
factors.source_paper: SSRN-The Trend is Our Friend Risk Parity, Momentum and Trend Following in Global Asset Allocation(2012).pdf

factors.definition: Trailing total return over 12-month lookback with 1-month skip period: r_mom = P(t-1)/P(t-12) - 1. Skip period mitigates short-term mean reversion and microstructure effects. Computed from price data; used as cross-sectional signal for multi-factor tilt.

Book-to-market ratio: BM = Book_Value(q) / Market_Cap(t), where q <= t is the most recent reporting date within a staleness threshold. Preferred over earnings-based measures for global applicability. Missing fundamentals result in neutral (zero) z-score.

Composite of profitability and balance-sheet strength: Quality = f(ROE, Debt/Equity, ...). Each component standardized cross-sectionally before aggregation. Captures both operating efficiency and financial conservatism.

Asset eligibility determined by minimum average daily trading volume (ADV) threshold observed at t-1. Assets below threshold excluded from investable universe. State-dependent constraint that adjusts factor exposure endogenously.
Asset eligibility conditioned on volatility proxy observed at t-1. High-volatility assets may be excluded to control portfolio fragility. Part of state-dependent universe selection framework.
Observable measure of cross-sectional market breadth at t-1. Used as state variable for dynamic eligibility constraint. Determines feasible asset set for portfolio construction.
Exponentially weighted downside deviation: E[R^2 * 1_{R<0}] where R is excess return. Exponentially smoothed with halflife of 10 trading days. Preferred risk measure focusing on downside losses.
Ratio of exponentially weighted mean return to exponentially weighted downside deviation, with 20-day halflife. Return measure for JM regime detection.
Ratio of exponentially weighted mean return to exponentially weighted downside deviation, with 60-day halflife. Longer halflife mitigates noise in return measures for jump model regime detection.

Jump model identifies bull/bear market regimes using 3 features (DD10, Sortino20, Sortino60) derived from excess returns. Enhances regime persistence via jump penalty at state transitions, unlike HMM which relies solely on return volatility. Optimal parameters updated every 6 months over 3000-day training window.
